      - term: United Kingdom
      - definition:
        - text: "The UK handles unlicensed medicines by a different route. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may be supplied to meet one patient's special needs, made to a prescriber's specification by a manufacturer that holds a specials licence, and it may not be advertised. The route (regulation 167): One patient, one prescriber, an unsolicited order. Made to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under their direct care. No advertisement may be published. Who makes it: A manufacturer with a specials licence. The site is inspected for good manufacturing practice; the product itself is otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy. A pharmacist may also prepare a medicine in a registered pharmacy against a prescription. Special need: The patient's clinical need. MHRA's examples include an intolerance or allergy to an ingredient, or an inability to swallow solid doses. Cost, convenience and operational needs do not count. MHRA's order of preference: Licensed, then off-label, then imported, then special. A UK-licensed medicine comes first, even used off-label; then one licensed in its country of origin; then a UK special. Least acceptable are products that are not medicines where they are made, such as supplements. Responsibility: The prescriber's. Be satisfied the evidence supports safety and efficacy, take responsibility for the prescription and the follow-up, record your reasons, and explain them to the patient when the use is not routine. GMC, MHRA and GPhC guidance say this; nurse prescribers work within the NMC Code. Cost and convenience never justify a special, and a licensed option that meets the need comes first. Dated to the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 and MHRA guidance as read on 25 September 2026."
        - generic: "Source: The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1916), regulation 167 — Supply to fulfil special patient needs · The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1916), regulation 46 — Requirement for authorisation · Medicines Act 1968, section 10 — Exemptions for pharmacists · The supply of unlicensed medicinal products ('specials') — MHRA Guidance Note 14 · Off-label or unlicensed use of medicines: prescribers' responsibilities (Drug Safety Update, April 2009, vol 2 issue 9) · Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices — Prescribing unlicensed medicines (paragraphs 102–108) · In practice: Guidance for pharmacist prescribers (updated April 2025) · The Code: professional standards of practice and behaviour for nurses, midwives and nursing associates — standard 18"
      - term: European Union
      - definition:
        - text: In the EU, a member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)). Medicines prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formulas) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formulas) are outside the Directive and need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).
        - generic: "Source: Directive 2001/83/EC on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use (consolidated text of 1 January 2025)"
      - term: Portugal
      - definition:
        - text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 July 2011), but it may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento). A physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004).
        - generic: "Source: Circular Informativa N.º 148/CD – Importação de medicamentos para uso pessoal · Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006, de 30 de agosto – Estatuto do Medicamento (regime jurídico dos medicamentos de uso humano), versão consolidada · Autorização de comercialização (AUE, AUE de lote e SAR) · Decreto-Lei n.º 95/2004, de 22 de abril – regula a prescrição e a preparação de medicamentos manipulados · Medicamentos manipulados – Inspeção de medicamentos manipulados"
      - term: Brazil
      - definition:
        - text: In Brazil, unregistered medicines may be imported only exceptionally, for strictly personal use and on a medical prescription, and import by any route is suspended when ANVISA publishes a specific prohibition; ANVISA stated in September 2025 that using an unregistered imported medicine is entirely the responsibility of the patient and the prescribing physician. ANVISA also stated in November 2024 that compounded medicines should be used only when the registered industrial product is unavailable in the dose or dosage form the patient needs.
        - generic: "Source: Anvisa informa sobre proibição de ingresso de canetas emagrecedoras no Brasil · Anvisa reforça orientações sobre importação de produtos para tratamento de saúde · Implantes hormonais: novas medidas vão impor mais rigor à manipulação"
      - term: United Arab Emirates
      - definition:
        - text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 exempts products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies from marketing approval (Art. 5(2)) and lets a physician prescribe a product never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval only when necessary, with no equivalent alternative available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and where permitted it limits prescribing to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and dispensing by compounding pharmacies to individual prescriptions. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026).
        - generic: "Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (28) of 2023 On the Establishment of the UAE Drug Corporation (official English translation) · Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation) · DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026) · DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)"
      - term: Saudi Arabia
      - definition: "Saudi context: FDA and 503A/503B rules are US comparison material, not a Saudi authorization pathway. Separate registration and indication from practitioner/facility scope, compounding, import and advertising. Check Saudi requirements for each decision; neither a certificate of analysis nor informed consent establishes product authorization. Detailed Saudi pathway review remains open."
    - paragraph: FDA's 503A bulks list and its categories are US law and policy and apply only in the US. In the other jurisdictions in this course, a medicine without a marketing authorisation reaches a patient as a pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply made on a prescription, and the prescriber answers for that choice.

    - generic: Set under US federal law and FDA policy; no other jurisdiction in this course applies them.

    - paragraph: "A 503A category means nothing outside the US: name the route your own law provides, and check it on the day."
